title: Homily II — Make your memory her dwelling

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, cols. 752-753 (PDF leaves 417-418)

source_text: Τί δὲ πρὸς τὸν τάφον ἡμεῖς ἀντιφήσομεν; Ἡ μὲν σὴ χάρις ἀνελλιπὴς καὶ ἀέναος, ἀλλ' οὐ τόποις ἡ θεία περιορίζεται δύναμις, οὐδὲ αἱ τῆς Θεομήτορος εὐεργεσίαι· εἰ γὰρ μόνῳ τῷ τύμβῳ περιεγράφοντο, ὀλίγοις ἂν ἡ δωρεὰ ἐπεθειάζετο. Νῦν δὲ ἐν πᾶσι τοῦ κόσμου τοῖς πέρασιν ἀφθόνως διανενέμηται. Τὴν μνήμην τοίνυν τὴν ἡμετέραν ταμεῖον τῆς Θεοτόκου κατασκευάσωμεν. Τοῦτο δὲ ἔσται πῶς; Παρθένος αὕτη, καὶ φιλοπάρθενος· ἁγνὴ πέφυκεν αὕτη, καὶ φίλαγνος. Ἂν οὖν σὺν τῷ σώματι καὶ τὴν μνήμην ἁγνίσωμεν, ἐνηυλισμένην τὴν αὐτῆς χάριν κτησόμεθα. Φεύγει γὰρ ἰλὺν ἅπασαν, καὶ τὰ βορβορώδη πάθη ἐκτρέπεται. Γαστριμαργίαν βδελύσσεται, τῆς αἰσχίστης πορνείας ἐχθραίνει τοῖς πάθεσι· ταύτης τοὺς μυσαροὺς λογισμοὺς ὡς ἐχιδνῶν φεύγει γεννήματα· λόγους αἰσχρούς τε καὶ εὐτραπέλους ἀπωθεῖται καὶ ᾄσματα· μῦρα πορνικὰ ἀποσείεται· μισεῖ θυμοῦ τὰ οἰδήματα, ἀπανθρωπίαν καὶ ἔριδας οὐ προσίεται· κενοδοξίαν τὴν ματαιόπονον ἀποστρέφεται· ὄγκῳ ὑπερηφανίας ἐχθρωδῶς ἀντιτάσσεται· μνησικακίαν μισεῖ, τὴν σωτηρίας ἀντίπαλον· πᾶσαν κακίαν ὡς ἰὸν θανατηφόρον λογίζεται, τούτων δὲ χαίρει τοῖς ἐναντίοις. Τὰ γὰρ ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων ἰάματα. Νηστείᾳ, καὶ ἐγκρατείᾳ, καὶ ψαλμικοῖς ἐπιτέρπεται ᾄσμασιν· ἁγνείᾳ, καὶ παρθενίᾳ, καὶ σωφροσύνῃ συγγήθεται. Καὶ πρὸς ταύτας εἰρήνην ἄγει ἀέναον, καὶ φιλοφρόνως ταύτας ἀσπάζεται. Εἰρήνην καὶ πρᾶον περιπτύσσεται φρόνημα, ἀγάπην, καὶ ἔλεον, καὶ ταπείνωσιν ὡς οἰκείας τροφοὺς ἀγκαλίζεται. Καὶ συνελόντα φάναι, ἐπὶ πάσῃ μὲν κακίᾳ, κατηφείᾳ δυσχεραίνουσα, πάσῃ δὲ ἀρετῇ ὡς οἰκείῳ χαρίσματι ἐπαγάλλεται. Εἰ οὖν τὰς προτέρας ἐκθύμως κακίας ἐκκλίνωμεν, τὰς δὲ ἀρετὰς πάσῃ σπουδῇ ἀγαπήσωμεν, καὶ ταύτας συνομίλους κτησώμεθα, θαμινὰ πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους οἰκέτας ἐλεύσεται, τὴν ἁπάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν σὺν αὐτῇ ἐφελκομένη ὁμήγυριν, καὶ Χριστὸν τὸν αὐτῆς Υἱὸν, καὶ τῶν ἁπάντων Βασιλέα καὶ Κύριον ἐνοικοῦντα ταῖς ἡμετέραις καρδίαις συμπαραλήψεται· ᾧ δόξα, τιμὴ, κράτος, μεγαλοσύνη τε καὶ μεγαλοπρέπεια, σὺν τῷ ἀνάρχῳ Πατρὶ, καὶ τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
pass_a_gloss: What shall we say in answer to the tomb? Your grace [is] unfailing (ἀνελλιπής) and ever-flowing (ἀέναος), but the divine power (δύναμις) is not bounded by places, nor the benefactions of the God-mother (Θεομήτωρ); for if they were circumscribed by the grave-mound (τύμβος) alone, to few would the gift (δωρεά) have been divinely granted. But now in all the ends (πέρατα) of the world it has been distributed ungrudgingly (ἀφθόνως). Our memory (μνήμη) then let us make ready [as] a chamber/storeroom (ταμεῖον) of the Theotokos. And this will be how? She [is] virgin and virgin-loving; she is pure (ἁγνή) and purity-loving (φίλαγνος). If then with the body we also purify (ἁγνίσωμεν) the memory, we shall possess her grace encamped/lodged [in us]. For she flees all slime (ἰλύς), and turns from the miry (βορβορώδη) passions. Gluttony she abhors, to the passions of most shameful fornication (πορνεία) she is hostile (ἐχθραίνει); its defiled (μυσαροί) thoughts (λογισμοί) she flees as offspring of vipers; shameful and jesting words she thrusts away, and songs; harlots' (πορνικά) perfumes she shakes off; she hates the swellings (οἰδήματα) of anger (θυμός); inhumanity and strifes (ἔριδες) she does not admit (προσίεται); vainglory (κενοδοξία) that labours in vain she turns from; the bulk (ὄγκος) of arrogance she opposes in enmity; remembrance of wrongs she hates, the adversary (ἀντίπαλος) of salvation; all evil (κακία) she reckons (λογίζεται) as death-bearing poison, and rejoices in the opposites of these. For opposites [are] cures (ἰάματα) of opposites. In fasting (νηστεία) and self-control (ἐγκράτεια) and psalm-songs she delights; with purity (ἁγνεία) and virginity (παρθενία) and temperance (σωφροσύνη) she rejoices together. And with these she keeps (ἄγει) ever-flowing peace, and kindly (φιλοφρόνως) greets (ἀσπάζεται) them. Peace and a meek (πρᾶον) mind (φρόνημα) she embraces; love (ἀγάπη) and mercy (ἔλεος) and humility (ταπείνωσις) as her own nurses she takes in her arms. And to speak summarily: at every evil, being vexed with dejection (κατήφεια), but in every virtue (ἀρετή) as in her own gift (χάρισμα) she exults. If then we ardently (ἐκθύμως) shun (ἐκκλίνωμεν) the former vices, and love the virtues with all zeal (σπουδή), and acquire them as companions (συνόμιλοι), frequently (θαμινά) to her own servants (οἰκέται) she will come, drawing along (ἐφελκομένη) with herself the assembly (ὁμήγυρις) of all the good things, and Christ her Son, King and Lord of all, indwelling (ἐνοικοῦντα) our hearts, she will bring along with [her]; to whom glory, honour, might (κράτος), greatness (μεγαλοσύνη) and magnificence, with the beginningless (ἄναρχος) Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of the ages. Amen.

lemmas.greek: ἐπεθειάζετο; R. ἐπεχωριάζετο, 'would have dwelt locally'

pass_b_english: And what shall we say in reply to the tomb? Your grace is unfailing and ever-flowing; but the power of God is not confined to places, nor are the benefits of the Mother of God. For if they were bounded by the tomb alone, the gift would have been bestowed on only a few. But now it has been shared out without stint in all the ends of the world. Let us then make our memory a chamber for the Mother of God. And how will this be? She is a virgin, and loves virginity; she is pure, and loves purity. If, then, together with the body we purify the memory too, we shall have her grace dwelling within us.

For she flees all filth and turns away from the muddy passions. She loathes gluttony; she is the enemy of the passions of most shameful fornication; its foul thoughts she flees as from a brood of vipers (Matthew 3:7). She thrusts away shameful and coarse words and songs (Ephesians 5:4). She shakes off the perfumes of harlots. She hates the swellings of anger; she will not admit inhumanity and strife. She turns away from vainglory that labours for nothing. She sets herself as an enemy against swollen pride. She hates the remembering of wrongs, the adversary of salvation. Every evil she counts as a deadly poison, and she rejoices in their opposites; for opposites are the cures of opposites. She delights in fasting and self-control and the songs of the Psalms; she rejoices with purity and virginity and sober self-restraint. With these she keeps unending peace and greets them warmly. Peace and a gentle mind she embraces; love and mercy and humility she takes in her arms, as her own nurses. In short, at every evil she is grieved and downcast, but in every virtue she exults as in a gift of her own.

If, then, we eagerly shun the vices named first and love the virtues with all zeal, and make them our companions, she will come often to her own servants, drawing with her the whole company of all good things; and she will bring with her Christ, her Son, the King and Lord of all, to dwell in our hearts. To him be glory, honour, might, greatness and majesty, with the Father who is without beginning, and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

choices.note: Unprinted allusions.
Cited: Matthew 3:7, because both γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν and fleeing (φεύγει;
Matthew φυγεῖν) appear together;
Ephesians 5:4, because αἰσχρ- and εὐτράπελ- (shameful talk and coarse jesting) stand together as in Paul.
Left uncited: the closing 'Christ ... to dwell in our hearts' fits Ephesians 3:17 (κατοικῆσαι τὸν Χριστὸν ...
ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν) and John 14:23 (the source note names John 14:23) but matches neither closely enough;
'deadly poison' (ἰὸς θανατηφόρος) shares two words with James 3:8 (of the tongue) but not its sense;
'harlots' perfumes' may glance at Proverbs 7:17.
Apparatus fn62: printed ἐπεθειάζετο ('would have been divinely bestowed on'), R.
ἐπεχωριάζετο ('would have stayed local to'); both give the same sense here, rendered 'the gift would have been bestowed on only a few'.
'ταμεῖον' rendered 'chamber' (inner room, store-room).
'μνήμη' kept as 'memory' (the remembrance in which she is kept).
'ὡς οἰκείας τροφοὺς' rendered 'as her own nurses' (τροφός = nurse);
Migne's Latin takes them as nurslings ('tanquam alumnas suas'), which ἀγκαλίζεται would also suit, but the Greek word means nurse.
'τὰς προτέρας κακίας' rendered 'the vices named first' (the vices listed before the virtues, set against τὰς δὲ ἀρετάς); it could also mean 'our former vices', but the Greek has no 'our'.
'λόγους αἰσχρούς τε καὶ εὐτραπέλους ...
καὶ ᾄσματα': both adjectives cover the songs too, so 'shameful and coarse words and songs'.
'ἐπὶ πάσῃ μὲν κακίᾳ, κατηφείᾳ δυσχεραίνουσα' is a participle without a finite verb in its clause; rendered 'she is grieved and downcast'.
'σωφροσύνη' rendered 'sober self-restraint' to keep it apart from ἁγνεία ('purity') and ἐγκράτεια ('self-control').
Doxology rendered as in Homily I (section 1.17): 'glory, honour, might, greatness and majesty ... now and always and to the ages of ages.
Amen.'
